speakers.label: PLENARY SPEAKER 2
speakers.name: Dr. Daniella Lagman-Eugenio
speakers.title: Shaping Resilient Institutions: Connecting Knowledge, Technology, and People
speakers.bio:
She is a graduate of Ateneo de Manila University with a degree in BS Management and currently serves as the Head of Product Marketing and Customer Success (PMCS) at CE-Logic, Inc.

She leads the team responsible for developing product-focused marketing, implementation, training, and customer engagement initiatives for CE-Logic's partner institutions. Through PMCS, she works to bridge the gap between providing access to academic resources and ensuring their meaningful adoption—helping institutions maximize their investments in digital solutions and achieve their desired outcomes in teaching, learning, and research.

Her work is particularly relevant as Philippine higher education continues to advance digital transformation, research and innovation, and the development of future-ready learning ecosystems. In this evolving landscape, she advocates for a customer success approach that goes beyond implementation by fostering sustained product adoption, meaningful engagement, and long-term institutional value.

Through her leadership of PMCS, Daniella works closely with higher education institutions to help ensure that technology and academic resources translate into measurable impact for their faculty, researchers, students, and the broader academic community.
speakers.abstract: As AI reshapes education and research, institutional resilience depends not only on technology but also on access to trusted knowledge, capable people, and sustainable systems. This session explores how institutions can build an inclusive research and learning ecosystem through digital solutions, quality information resources, capacity-building programs, and strategic partnerships. It will also highlight CE-Logic's role in connecting institutions with solutions and support that advance their academic, research, and innovation goals.

speakers.label: PLENARY SPEAKER 3
speakers.name: Dr. Ricardo BAGARINAO
speakers.title: A Double-Edged Transformation: The Paradox of AI and Sustainability in Education
speakers.bio: He has built a career that brings together teaching, academic leadership, environmental research, and the evolving field of open and digital learning. He joined the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) as a full-time faculty member in 2006, where he taught biology and related courses in the Faculty of Education and the Faculty of Management and Development Studies. His years at UPOU have taken him through various academic and administrative roles. He served as Program Chair of the PhD in Education, University Registrar, Dean of the Faculty of Education, and Director of the Center for Open and Digital Teaching and Learning. He currently serves as Assistant to the Chancellor for Sustainability and the Program Chair of the Doctor in Sustainability. His research interests reflect a continuing concern for the relationship between people, places, and the environment. These include landscape ecology, land use and land cover change, environmental management, disaster preparedness and risk reduction, and spatial analysis using geographic information systems. His work in open and distance education has likewise expanded his research into e-learning and open learning. He has published in peer-reviewed and indexed national and international journals and contributed chapters to books published locally and internationally. Behind these credentials is an academic journey that has moved across disciplines and institutions—from biology and environmental research to education, digital learning, and sustainability.
speakers.abstract: Education shapes sustainability direction while artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly transforms education and re-shapes knowledge creation, access, sharing, and application. Though AI offers new opportunities for more inclusive and sustainable education, it also operates with growing concerns about energy and resource consumption, environmental impacts, privacy, unequal access, and social inequality. The paper examines this double-edged transformation, challenging the assumption that technological innovation is always progressive or sustainable. It also explores how educators and institutions can navigate the tensions between innovation and responsibility, efficiency and ecological cost, personalization and privacy, access and inequality, and technological capability and human judgment. More importantly, it positions education not simply as a user of AI, but as a force that can shape how societies understand, govern, and use AI. The paper concludes that sustainable use of AI in education must go beyond technological adoption. It requires critical AI literacy, ethical responsibility, ecological awareness, and informed human judgment to ensure that AI contributes to more inclusive, responsible, and sustainable futures.

speakers.label: PLENARY SPEAKER 4
speakers.name: Dr. Mohd Erfino JOHARI
speakers.title: Human-Centred AI in Higher Education: From Intelligent Technology to Ethical, Inclusive and Future-Ready Universities
speakers.bio:
Dr. Mohd Erfino Johari is a Malaysian academic leader with over 30 years of experience in higher education governance, international academic diplomacy, public service, and corporate leadership. He currently serves as Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic and Internationalisation) at Universiti Poly-Tech Malaysia (UPTM), where he leads academic transformation, global partnerships, dual-degree initiatives and institutional internationalisation strategies. He previously served as Director of Industrial Linkages and Academic Internationalisation (ILAI) and contributes actively to university governance through Senate committees and scholarly editorial boards.

His career spans significant roles within the Malaysian Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Higher Education, including service as Education Attaché for Malaysia in the United Kingdom and Ireland and later as Director & Counsellor (Education) at the Malaysian High Commission in New Zealand, advancing bilateral academic cooperation and cross-border education initiatives. He also held senior corporate leadership roles as Chief Corporate Officer and Acting Chief Marketing Officer, contributing expertise in strategic governance, institutional branding and organisational performance.

Internationally engaged, he serves as Visiting Professor/Lecturer at Universidad De Ixtlahuaca Mexico, Universitas PGRI Indonesia, Universitas Nahdlatul Ulama Indonesia and Universitas Ahmad Dahlan Indonesia. Appointed as International Research Fellow at Shinawatra International University Thailand and the International Cultural Communication Center Malaysia (ICCCM). He was invited as Keynote Speaker at SCTE2025 in Cairo, Egypt. He currently holds ten research grants including the FRGS (MOHE) and published more than 20 indexed journal articles for the last 3 years across Scopus, Web of Science, ERA, and MyCite. His research has earned Best Paper Awards at ICAR2023 and ICAR2025, as well as the Best Presenter Award at ICAR2025. He holds a PhD from UPSI in Education, a Master's degree from OUM, and a Bachelor's degree from University of Jordan, with additional qualifications in education, management and counselling. His research focuses on Geo-Islamica education, Shariah-compliant governance, higher education policy, internationalisation strategy and nation-building. Guided by principles of integrity, inclusivity, and service, he continues to advance globally connected universities and future-ready graduates through scholarship, diplomacy, and strategic academic leadership.
speakers.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) rapidly redefines the global educational landscape, higher education institutions stand at a critical crossroads. The mandate facing academic leaders is no longer merely adopting intelligent technologies, but strategically steering them to serve human flourishing, educational equity and institutional resilience. This keynote outlines a comprehensive framework for embedding Human-Centred AI (HCAI) across university ecosystems by integrating the universal ethical principles of Maqasid Shariah (the higher objectives of Islamic law). By translating these profound objectives, the preservation of values, human dignity, intellect, future generations and equitable resources, into a modern techno-academic context, the presentation offers a robust philosophical and practical model for AI governance. Drawing from strategic initiatives at Universiti Poly-Tech Malaysia (UPTM), the session addresses five interconnected pillars: ethical governance, authentic assessment, inclusive pedagogy, responsible innovation and sustainable institutional transformation. Ultimately, this presentation advocates for a balanced academic ecosystem where intelligent technology and human wisdom co-exist to prepare ethical leaders for an automated world.

speakers.bio:
Dr. Juvy A. Balbarona is a professor and former Chairman of the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the University of the Philippines Diliman. She completed her B.S. and M.S. degrees in Mechanical Engineering and her Ph.D. in Energy Engineering at UP Diliman, later serving as the College of Engineering's Associate Dean for Student Affairs.

She specializes in thermal systems modelling, surface modification for heat transfer enhancement, and energy modeling. Her current research focuses on engineering metal surfaces to enhance pool boiling, application of nature inspired texture for improve water harvesting and dehumidification, and oscillating heat pipes. Currently, she is the head of the Nanomaterials and Heat Transfer Laboratory at the ME Department in UP Diliman.

speakers.title: Are We (Still) Human? Or Are We Dancers (to the Beat of AI)?
speakers.bio: Dr. Jared Aaron R. Cruz is an architect by profession, a project manager by specialization, and an educator by vocation. A full-time faculty member for 14 years at the Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, he concurrently serves as an Assistant Professor and Dean of its College of Architecture and Sustainable Built Environments. A Doctor of Philosophy in the Designed and Built Environment from the University of the Philippines Diliman College of Architecture and a Certified BERDE Professional for Districts, he has research interests in sustainability, resilience, architectural history, and built heritage conservation. Prior to his tenure in the academe, he engaged in residential and commercial design and construction consultancy services after passing and ranking 4th in the June 2010 Architect's Licensure Exam.

speakers.label: STEA KEYNOTE SPEAKER 3
speakers.name: Dr. Magin Benedict FERRER
speakers.title: Project Resin Green: Overview of Initiative and Focus on the Increased Efficiency of DUV Photolithography of Chitosan Bioresist with New Water-soluble PAGs
speakers.bio:
Magin Benedict F. Ferrer is currently a postdoctoral researcher at the Institut de Science de Matériaux de Mulhouse (IS2M) in France. His research interests include photochemistry, radiation detection and photolithography.

After obtaining his Bachelor's degrees in Chemistry (2018) and Materials Science and Engineering (2019) at the Ateneo de Manila University, he moved to Europe for his postgraduate studies. Under the SERP+ Erasmus Mundus Program, he obtained Master's degrees in Chemistry from the Paris-Saclay University, France, and in Materials Science and Technology from the University of Genoa, Italy in 2021.

In 2024, he finished a double-degree PhD in Chemistry under joint supervision from the PPSM laboratory of Paris-Saclay University, and the Photonic and Reactive Molecular Science Laboratory of the Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan.
speakers.abstract: Microchip production constitutes a very important industry; however, current fabrication processes use chemicals that pose health risks and environmental hazards during disposal. The RESIN GREEN Project aims to develop new resist materials and nanometrology methods with the goal of reducing the ecological footprint of digital technology. Bio-sourced polymers have been studied to aid in the transition to eco-friendlier processes. The polysaccharide chitosan has shown promise as a water-soluble photoresist in photolithography at 193 nm (Deep UV), already behaving as a positive tone resist via chain scission of its glycosidic bonds. A commercial photoacid generator (PAG 0) was tested to enhance this effect; however, its sensitivity is still lower than industrial standards. Two new fluorine-free water-soluble PAGs conceptually inspired by commercially available sulfonium salts were synthesized and incorporated in the chitosan resist platform significantly improving the sensitivity of the resulting films in DUV photolithography by reducing the dose-to-clear value and demonstrating the possibility for photomask patterning.

speakers.label: STEA KEYNOTE SPEAKER 4
speakers.name: Prof. Larry V. Padilla
speakers.title: Beyond the Surface: A Unitive Worldview Approach to Flood System Dynamics in Barangay Landayan, San Pedro City, Laguna
speakers.bio:
Larry V. Padilla is an Associate Professor of the Biology Department, College of Science, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila (PLM). He previously served as the Director of the University Research Center, the Department Chair of the Biology Department and the College Secretary of the College of Science of this university. His research interests span from harmful algal bloom mitigation and ecology, aquatic ecology, environmental assessments and monitoring, natural products, sustainability science to chronobiology of organisms. He obtained his BSc in Biology degree from PLM and his MSc in Marine Science (maj. in Marine Biology) degree from The Marine Science Institute of the University of the Philippines (UP-MSI) in Diliman. He is currently pursuing a Doctorate degree in Sustainability from the University of the Philippines – Open University after taking some course work in PhD in Biology.

Larry is an educator, a marine and environmental scientist, and a researcher. As a researcher, he was able to publish several research works in scientific journals indexed in Web of Science, Scopus, and ASEAN Citation index. He is an associate member of the National Research Council of the Philippines (NRCP) among other professional and technical organizations and was also part of the pioneering batch of the National Academy of Science and Technology (NAST)- Future Science Leaders. He was one of the three recipients of the Most Outstanding Faculty Award during PLM's 50th Golden Anniversary and the Nemenzo Award in one of the National Symposium in Marine Science. Prior to teaching in PLM, he also worked as an Environmental Scientist for AECOM, a multinational consultancy firm, and as a University Research Associate at the Marine Science Institute in UP Diliman. He has also joined oceanographic research cruises in the past that traversed the inner and eastern seas of the Philippines, was involved in several environmental consultancy works, and is also serving as a biology consultant tasked as an item validator and an item writer for national admission examinations.
speakers.abstract:
Carl Addeb1,2, Lounelle Godinez1,3, Larry V. Padilla1,4*, Stephenn Rabano1,5, Christopher Niño Santos1,3, Roxanne Selmo1,6, Roda Valenzuela1

1University of the Philippines - Open University, Los Baños, Laguna, Philippines

2Polytechnic University of the Philippines - San Pedro Campus, San Pedro, Laguna, Philippines

Flooding in the Philippines is a systemic and persistent problem affecting communities. One area consistently experiencing its devastating impacts is Barangay Landayan, San Pedro City in Laguna, a lakeshore community. It has been reported that flood waters in several areas have not subsided for several months. The root cause/s of this wicked problem has not been definitively determined, prompting ineffective actions and measures to address the issue. This study sought to determine the causes of flooding in the area to identify potential solutions and adaptations using the Unitive Worldview Framework. Geospatial analyses of selected historical maps and images to trace changes in green spaces, ecosystems, land area, and waterways, as supported by secondary data, were performed using QGIS software. Two focused discussions (FGD) were also conducted to obtain crucial insights from key informants. Findings revealed that flooding may be attributed to encroachment of waters caused by lakeshore subsidence, wetland conversion to built-up areas, loss of green ecosystem, and obstruction of waterways. Moreover, FGDs revealed anthropocentric causes of flooding clustered into three themes: problematic multi-partite planning and execution, questionable strategic disaster mitigation investments, and failed urban resilience. This study revealed that flooding in Barangay Landayan is multi-causal and a complex problem that requires appropriate and holistic interventions, mitigation measures, and adaptations by the stakeholders, with some detailed in this paper.

speakers.name: Dr. Aldrin BONTO
speakers.title: Exploring Food Structure and Functionalities: Unveiling Insights Through Material Science Perspectives
speakers.abstract: Food matrices are multiscale, heterogeneous materials whose physicochemical and functional properties emerge from complex interactions among biopolymers, water, micronutrients, and processing-induced structural transformations. This presentation examines food systems through a material science framework, focusing on structure–property–function relationships across molecular, microstructural, and macroscopic scales. Using cereal grains, starch-rich matrices, plant-derived flours, and polysaccharide-based materials as representative systems, the effects of emerging and conventional processing strategies, including ultrasonication, atmospheric cold plasma, germination, and fortification, on material organization and functionality are discussed. Particular attention is given to changes in surface characteristics, crystallinity, molecular interactions, thermal transitions, rheological behavior, hydration, texture, and nutrient accessibility. Complementary characterization using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, microscopy, differential scanning calorimetry, thermogravimetric analysis, particle and surface characterization, and multivariate chemometric approaches enables mechanistic interpretation of processing-induced transformations. The discussion further extends material science concepts toward engineered starch-based systems, highlighting how controlled structural modification can tailor mechanical and functional performance. This materials-driven approach provides a mechanistic platform for linking processing, structure, and functionality, supporting the rational design of next-generation food materials with improved nutritional and sustainability attributes.

speakers.title: WHEN EVERYONE HAS AI, WHAT BECOMES THE COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE?
speakers.bio:
Leo D. Manansala, PhD is a higher-education executive, management scholar, and researcher with more than two decades of experience in academic leadership, teaching, research, and institutional administration. He currently serves as Vice Dean of the College of Professional and Graduate Studies and concurrently leads the School of Governance, Public Service, and Corporate Leadership at De La Salle University–Dasmariñas, where he is also a faculty member in Business Management.

Dr. Manansala's research interests span strategic management, digital transformation, business analytics, organizational development, human capital, ESG and sustainability, entrepreneurship, consumer behavior, and technology-mediated decision-making. His research has examined digital transformation and organizational innovation, financial and operational performance, human capital, ESG and sustainability, enterprise resilience, and the influence of social media and digital platforms on consumer behavior.

He serves as Editor-in-Chief of the Lasallian Journal of Business and Tourism and as an Academic Editor for PLOS ONE. He also serves as a peer reviewer for various reputable international journals, in addition to his work as a research mentor, graduate research supervisor, and academic leader.

His current research agenda increasingly focuses on the intersection of technology, sustainability, and human behavior, including AI-enabled transformation, sustainable consumption, digitalization and cultural tourism, sustainability disclosure, and technology's influence on consumer choices.

Through his academic, research, and leadership work, Dr. Manansala is particularly interested in one overarching question: How can technological innovation be transformed into sustainable value for organizations, institutions, and communities?
speakers.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming ubiquitous across organizations, universities, businesses, and communities. As access to generative AI becomes increasingly democratized, a critical strategic question emerges: when everyone has AI, what becomes the competitive advantage?

This keynote argues that AI itself will not remain the primary source of competitive advantage. Rather, the differentiating factor will be the ability of individuals and organizations to transform access to AI into meaningful, sustainable, and inclusive value. The central proposition is simple: AI is the enabler. Capability is the differentiator. Sustainable value is the test.

Drawing from research on digital transformation, organizational innovation, human capital, ESG, digitalization, technology-mediated consumer behavior, and enterprise resilience, the presentation examines how technological capabilities interact with organizational conditions, institutional environments, human judgment, and societal outcomes. Evidence from research on generative AI productivity further illustrates both the potential of AI to enhance performance and the risks of relying on AI without sufficient human judgment and critical evaluation.

The keynote proposes an AI Sustainability Test centered on a single question: Does AI strengthen human capability? Does it create sustainable economic value? Does it expand social opportunity? What are its environmental costs? And is it supported by responsible institutional governance?

Ultimately, the challenge is no longer simply how to adopt AI, but how to use it wisely. For researchers, educators, business leaders, and policymakers, the imperative is to move beyond asking whether AI works toward asking when it works, for whom, at what cost, and toward what kind of future. The future competitive advantage may therefore belong not to those with the most AI, but to those who can use AI without losing purpose, inclusion, resilience, and humanity.

Advances in cancer genomics are transforming our understanding of cancer biology and creating new opportunities for precision medicine. However, the benefits of genomic innovation remain unevenly distributed, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where limited genomic data, research infrastructure, and access to advanced technologies can hinder translation into clinical practice. In the Philippines, these challenges highlight the need for approaches that are not only scientifically innovative but also sustainable, inclusive, and responsive to local health priorities. This talk explores how cancer genomics can move from laboratory discoveries toward better and more accessible healthcare for Filipinos. Drawing from research on molecular alterations in Filipino cancer patients, particularly those with young-onset colorectal cancer, it highlights the importance of generating local genomic data to better understand cancer within the Philippine population. It also examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can support the analysis of complex genomic and clinical data, facilitate biomarker discovery, and advance precision medicine. Beyond technological innovation, the talk emphasizes the importance of sustainable research infrastructure, responsible data use, local capacity-building, and inclusive innovation to ensure that Filipino patients are adequately represented and can benefit from advances in cancer genomics. Ultimately, integrating science, AI, sustainability, and inclusivity can help bridge the gap between laboratory discoveries and practical, equitable, and locally relevant healthcare solutions.

speakers.title: Designing Sustainable Bioinks: Biomaterials as the Foundation of a Bioprinting Ecosystem
speakers.bio:
Mary Stephanie S. Carranza is Co-Founder and Managing Director of BIOMATS PH, a Philippine biotechnology startup developing bioprinting technologies and biomaterials for biomedical research. She also serves as Head of the Biomedical Research Unit (BRU) at the Clinical and Translational Research Institute of The Medical City – Ortigas, where she leads research programs supporting translational biomedical innovation. Ms. Carranza is currently leading her own DOST project and is a consultant to several government-funded tissue engineering projects. She previously served as Laboratory Manager (University Researcher II) at the Philippine Genome Center's Protein, Proteomics, and Metabolomics Facility, supporting national research initiatives in metabolomics and proteomics.

Carranza has over eight years of research experience in biomaterials, tissue engineering, metabolomics, and translational biomedical research. Her expertise includes biomaterial modification, bioink development, 3D cell culture, and 3D bioprinting for next-generation in vitro models. She also serves as a consultant to several tissue engineering projects, with a particular focus on 3D bioprinting and bio fabrication.

Her honors include the Leaders in Innovation Fellowship of the Royal Academy of Engineering (2026), the Short-Stay Scholar Award from the Japan Student Services Organization (2025), and recognition as a finalist in the 2021 Merck Young Scientist Award in the Philippines.

Carranza holds a B.S. in Biochemistry and an M.S. in Chemistry, specializing in biomaterials, from De La Salle University - Manila. She also pursued graduate training in biomaterials at Osaka University as a Japanese government (MEXT) scholar.
speakers.abstract:
Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting sits at the intersection of biomaterials, engineering, and biology, offering new opportunities to develop physiologically relevant in vitro models and regenerative tissue technologies. However, the success of a bioprinted construct is not determined by the printer alone. The choice of polymer, method of processing, and design of biomaterials fundamentally influence printability, structural fidelity, cell compatibility, and ultimately the biological function of the printed tissue.

This talk will explore key considerations in bioink design, from the intrinsic properties of biomaterials and their rheological behavior to crosslinking, degradation, mechanical performance, and interactions with cells. Examples will illustrate how these considerations change depending on the intended application, from scaffold-based tissue regeneration to the development of reproducible in vitro disease and drug-testing models.

Beyond individual bioinks and applications, the discussion will consider sustainability as an ecosystem-level challenge. Developing accessible, adaptable, and locally relevant biomaterials and bioprinting technologies can reduce dependence on imported materials and equipment while enabling researchers to build capabilities suited to regional needs. Establishing shared expertise, characterization infrastructure, standardized approaches, and collaborations across academia, industry, and healthcare can create a more sustainable pathway for bioprinting research and translation.

Ultimately, advancing bioprinting in the region requires more than developing better materials or printers, it requires building an ecosystem that allows researchers to move from biomaterial design to functional biological models and, eventually, regenerative applications.

speakers.title: Simulating the Future: An Outcomes-based and Sustainable Approach to Preparing Future-Ready Nurses
speakers.bio:
Dr. David Paul R. Ramos is an Associate Professor III and former Dean of the College of Nursing at the Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila. He holds a Doctor of Philosophy in Nursing Education, a Master's in Nursing Education from the University of the Philippines Manila, and a Master of Arts in Nursing major in Nursing Administration. A registered nurse with clinical experience in perioperative nursing, he has devoted more than two decades to nursing practice, education, research, and academic leadership.

Dr. Ramos has authored and co-authored studies on nursing education, academic motivation, organizational commitment, exercise dependence, and data privacy. His scholarly work has been presented at national and international conferences, including the Sigma Nursing International Nursing Research Congress in Seattle, Washington. He is an Associate Member of the National Research Council of the Philippines and previously served as a Board Director of the Philippine Nurses Association–NCR Zone 1 and Vice President of the Sigma Theta Tau International Honor Society of Nursing–Phi Gamma Chapter.

His professional interests include simulation-based nursing education, perioperative nursing, curriculum development, evidence-based teaching, research, and educational innovation. Through his work, he continues to advocate for transformative learning experiences that prepare future nurses to provide safe, competent, compassionate, and responsive care.
speakers.abstract: Preparing future-ready nurses requires educational approaches that can address limited clinical placements, resource constraints, and the increasing complexity of healthcare practice. This plenary presentation examines simulation-based nursing education as an outcomes-based, innovative, and sustainable strategy for strengthening clinical readiness and preparing nurses to contribute to resilient and inclusive communities. This presentation describes the integration of a structured, low-fidelity perioperative simulation module into third-year Adult Health Nursing. Guided by Bondy's Clinical Performance Path Model, the module was designed to support students' progression from assisted toward supervised clinical performance. It combined prebriefing, skills stations, role-based operating-room scenarios, structured debriefing, and competency-based evaluation. Learners managed simulated situations involving breaks in sterile technique, incorrect surgical counts, intraoperative bleeding, patient-safety risks, prioritization, and interdisciplinary communication. Pilot qualitative validation based on student narratives indicated that participants exposed to simulation perceived stronger clinical understanding, confidence, procedural skills, communication, teamwork, and ability to connect theory with practice. Narratives from students without simulation exposure reflected greater dependence on lectures, return demonstrations, observation, and clinical-instructor guidance, together with continuing difficulty applying knowledge in realistic situations. These findings support the curricular value of structured simulation while remaining limited to students' reported experiences rather than controlled measures of effectiveness. Such applications must remain ethical, transparent, culturally responsive, and educator-guided. By enabling safe repetition, reducing exclusive dependence on scarce clinical placements, and permitting locally developed, resource-conscious learning experiences, simulation can advance sustainability and educational inclusion.

speakers.abstract: Higher education is increasingly challenged to prepare students for rapidly evolving artificial intelligence environments while ensuring that learning remains practical, ethical, and industry-relevant. Work-integrated learning offers an opportunity to move beyond theoretical AI literacy by involving students directly in authentic operational, governance, and leadership activities. Drawing on the student-driven operational model developed for the Borneo AI Summit 2026, this presentation highlights how university students can contribute meaningfully to live industry and regional innovation ecosystems. Student Virtual Assistants are embedded within functional areas including commercial research, ticketing, public relations and media production, protocol, certification logistics, data management, and structured operational handovers. Through these responsibilities, students gain practical exposure to leadership, communication, teamwork, data privacy, PDPA compliance, responsible AI practices, and cross-border collaboration. The model also demonstrates how higher education institutions can strengthen university-industry partnerships by positioning students as accountable contributors rather than passive observers. By connecting experiential learning with regional priorities such as Inclusive Intelligence and cross-border AI collaboration, the approach supports graduate readiness and ASEAN talent development. A scalable framework is proposed for educators seeking to integrate live industry projects into university learning while strengthening responsible AI leadership and regional innovation capacity.

speakers.bio: Zarah Dane R. Dimagmaliw-Tan is an Assistant Professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman. Currently on study leave to pursue a doctorate in Language Sciences at the Université de Rouen Normandie, her dissertation aims to study and propose a sustainable training program for DepEd French-language teachers. She holds two master's degrees: one in French Translation from the UP Diliman and one in language didactics from the Université Sorbonne Nouvelle. She is an active member of the Association des professeurs de français aux Philippines where she served as president from 2011-2018 and 2024-2025.
speakers.abstract:
How is Artificial Intelligence transforming foreign language learning and teaching? Before ChatGPT, students were already using AI in the form of machine translation tools like Google Translate to understand or produce a text in the target foreign language that is beyond their current proficiency level. But for this, the student needs to be able to understand or produce a text in another language where the student has a higher proficiency in. Now, with generative AI such as ChatGPT, there is no need even for that. Students can simply transform what they need to accomplish into a prompt that the AI can execute.

Yet AI should not be viewed solely as a shortcut or a threat to language learning. When used critically and appropriately, AI can become a powerful tool for learning, teaching, and creating more inclusive and innovative language-learning environments. This raises important questions: Is AI use in language learning sustainable? What does sustainable AI use mean in foreign language learning? How can educators harness AI without undermining the development of genuine linguistic competence, critical thinking, and learner autonomy? And how can AI help transform foreign language learning communities into resilient, inclusive, and future-ready communities?

This keynote explores these questions by examining the opportunities and challenges presented by AI in foreign language education through personal experiences in the field and by reflecting on how its responsible integration can contribute to more sustainable and innovative approaches to language learning and teaching.

speakers.label: EASS Keynote Speaker 3
speakers.name: Dr. Stephanie Marie R. COO
speakers.title: Reading Agency in Clothing: Sartorial History as a Lens for Resilient, Inclusive Futures
speakers.bio: Stephanie Marie R. Coo is an Associate Professor of History at the Ateneo de Manila University (Philippines) and a researcher at CHAM – Centro de Humanidades, Universidade Nova de Lisboa (Portugal). She holds a PhD in History from Université Nice Sophia Antipolis (France) and has held research fellowships at the Universidad de Granada (Spain), NOVA School of Law, Universidade Nova de Lisboa (Portugal) and Ruhr-Universität Bochum (Germany), including a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowship. She is the award-winning author of Clothing the Colony: Nineteenth-Century Philippine Sartorial Culture, 1820–1896, recipient of the IIAS-ICAS International Book Prize for Best Book in Humanities (Netherlands, 2021), National Book Award and the John C. Kaw Prize for Best Book in History (Philippines, 2022). Her second book, Seams of Sedition: Sartorial Symbols in José Rizal´s Noli Me Tángere (Ateneo de Naga University Press, 2025), expands the study to clothing, literature, and resistance in late colonial Philippines. It was launched internationally at the Leipzig Book Fair 2025, Frankfurt Book Fair - Philippines as Guest of Honor Nation 2025, Berlin Ibero-American Institute (Berlin, 2025), Biblioteca Palácio Galveias (Lisbon, 2025), and at the National Museum of Fine Arts (Manila, 2026). Her work explores the intersections of material culture, dress, gender, and colonial society in the nineteenth-century Philippines and the broader Iberian world.
speakers.abstract:
Drawing on two book-length studies of Philippine sartorial history, Clothing the Colony: Nineteenth-Century Philippine Sartorial Culture, 1820–1896 and Seams of Sedition: Sartorial Symbols in José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere, this keynote examines clothing as an underused archive of human agency, identity, and adaptation, treating dress not as decorative or peripheral but as a primary source through which marginalized groups negotiated power, expressed dignity, and shaped their own narratives within colonial systems and their aftermaths.

Organized around several guiding questions, this seeks to address how individuals exercise agency within systems of imposed regulation, whether sartorial, colonial, or technological. What can material and literary details reveal about identity formation that formal records omit? How did power, everyday practice, and encoded meaning intersect in the lived experience of colonial subjects, and how might that intersection be traced in other systems of constraint? And, most centrally for this audience, how might historical methods of reading agency, resilience, and adaptation inform the design, evaluation, and study of present-day inclusive systems and emerging technologies? Though these questions are first posed in a nineteenth-century colonial context, they are deliberately framed to travel forward, since any system that regulates behavior through unstated rules, whether a sumptuary ordinance or an algorithm, raises the same basic question of who is served and who must quietly adapt.

To answer these questions, the study is grounded in a layered theoretical framework spanning power, practice, and meaning. Pierre Bourdieu's theory of cultural and symbolic capital and Michel Foucault's analysis of power and the disciplined body explain how dress functioned as both currency and mechanism of colonial stratification. James C. Scott's concept of everyday resistance and Michel de Certeau's distinction between imposed strategies and improvised tactics inform how small, low-visibility sartorial choices are read as meaningful acts of agency within constraint. Marcel Mauss's theory of gift and reciprocal exchange and Daniel Miller's work in material culture studies anchor clothing as socially constitutive rather than merely decorative, while Roland Barthes's semiotics of fashion, Homi Bhabha's theory of colonial hybridity, and Jacques Derrida's method of deconstruction provide the interpretive tools for reading garments and texts as unstable, layered sign systems.

Guided by this framework, the underlying research draws on an extensive body of primary sources, including nineteenth-century artworks, studio and family photographs, period newspapers, foreign travelers' accounts, novels, and surviving garments, cross-referenced with one another and combined with close literary reading of Rizal's prose, allowing material and textual evidence to illuminate one another. This body of evidence shows how clothing functioned as both a tool of colonial control and a medium through which Filipinos exercised choice and self-determination, and how literary and historical sources, read together, reveal the ways sartorial detail encodes social hierarchy, aspiration, and emerging national identity, with agency often expressed in small, easily overlooked acts rather than overt confrontation.

In seeking to answer these questions, the keynote aims to establish clothing and literature as rigorous sources for understanding social agency, to model an interdisciplinary method linking material culture, literary analysis, and history, and to translate these historical insights into a practical framework for evaluating inclusivity in contemporary innovation. In line with the conference theme, "Shaping Resilient Futures: AI, Sustainability, and Inclusive Innovation," the keynote extends this framework to invite researchers across disciplines to bring the same attentiveness to overlooked detail, adaptation, and agency when designing, deploying, and studying technologies and systems meant to serve plural communities.

An Igorot born and raised in Baguio City with ancestral roots from the Mountain Provinces. Dr. Jularbal received his PhD from the UPD Tri-College under its Philippine studies program. His research and published works include Cordilleran and highland public policy, Northern Local Language and literatures, as well as indigenous traditions and material culture. He is currently Dean of the College of Arts and Communication, University of the Philippines Baguio where he is also faculty of the department of language and literature and researcher for the cordillera studies center (CSC).

Currently, the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a tool in bolstering representation capabilities of indigenous communities in the Cordillera has received much prominence and fashionability. From image generation to song and text composition etc., AI technology has taken indigenous representation to a wider audience with vast interactive capability, but despite all this, AI has proven itself to be revolutionary on a double-edged perspective, straddling a thin line between heritage preservation and misrepresentation.

My keynote presentation will take into consideration the duality of AI as potential conservator and destroyer of cultural heritage and as such, posing ethical and technical issues, risks, and challenges. At present, both Indigenous representation and Artificial intelligence are rapidly evolving and to see the intersection between the two is indeed inevitable. The potential of AI in the promotion of Indigenous knowledge and heritage constructs also exists with the reality that such a promotion can lead to misinformation, misrepresentation, and eventual erosion of cultural and life ways for many indigenous communities.

speakers.title: Beyond Efficiency: Harnessing Generative AI for Research Excellence in Philippine HEIs
speakers.bio: Dr. Feorillo A. Demeterio III is a Distinguished Full Professor of the Department of Filipino, College of Liberal Arts, De La Salle University, and Head of the Matter and Memory Research Laboratory. He has extensive experience in research administration, capacity building, and scholarly mentoring, being the Executive Director of the University's Research and Grants Management Office for more than a decade now. In recent years, Dr. Demeterio has developed particular expertise in AI-assisted research mentoring, especially in guiding faculty members, graduate students, and researchers in the strategic use of generative AI across different stages of the research process. His mentoring work covers the development and refinement of research titles and problems, systematic and scoping literature reviews, conceptual and theoretical frameworks, research design, qualitative and quantitative analysis, article extraction, results-and-discussion writing, journal targeting, and manuscript development. He has designed and facilitated numerous workshops and writeshops on AI-assisted research and scholarly publication. Dr. Demeterio is the author or co-author of several books and more than a hundred scholarly articles in hermeneutics, cultural studies, Philippine studies, and Filipino philosophy. He has held visiting research appointments in Washington, D.C., and Hong Kong, and is a co-founder of the Andrew Gonzalez Philippine Citation Index.
speakers.abstract:
Full Professor,Department of Filipino, College of Liberal Arts, De La Salle University

Executive Director University Research and Grants Management Office, De La Salle University

Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming research from a largely individual and sequential process into a more interactive, iterative, and computationally augmented form of knowledge production. This keynote argues that the value of generative AI for Philippine higher education institutions extends far beyond efficiency and automation. Properly integrated, generative AI can strengthen research excellence by supporting researchers across the research cycle—from problem formulation, literature searching and synthesis, conceptual and theoretical framing, research design, data analysis, interpretation, visualization, and scholarly writing to publication preparation. It can likewise enhance research mentoring by enabling more sustained feedback, scaffolding methodological reasoning, diagnosing weaknesses in manuscripts, and helping mentors guide larger and more diverse groups of researchers. The presentation further examines how generative AI is reshaping the research ecosystem by changing expectations regarding researcher competencies, mentoring practices, publication workflows, institutional research support, and research governance. It argues that Philippine HEIs must move from defensive or purely regulatory responses toward deliberate institutional adaptation. This requires developing AI literacy, ethical and transparent research practices, appropriate governance frameworks, and AI-assisted research mentoring systems. The central challenge is therefore not whether Philippine HEIs should use generative AI, but how they can harness it responsibly to expand research capacity, improve scholarly quality, and strengthen their participation in global knowledge production.

As a session members, you are responsible for ensuring that the session proceeds smoothly, adhering to the schedule, and fostering a productive and respectful environment for both presenters and attendees. Your leadership will contribute significantly to the overall effectiveness and professionalism of the conference.
Guidelines for Session Members

Pre-Session Preparation Arrive at the designated session room at least 15 minutes before the session begins. Use this time to familiarize yourself with the room setup and the schedule. Verify the attendance of all scheduled presenters by cross-checking the list provided in the conference program. If any presenter is absent, please notify the conference staff immediately.

Starting the Session. Begin the session promptly at the scheduled time. As the host, welcome the attendees warmly and introduce the session's theme. Clearly state the ground rules at the outset, emphasizing the importance of adhering to the time limits for presentations and the Q&A segment. Highlight that respecting the schedule is crucial for maintaining the flow of the session and allowing equal opportunity for all presenters.
For online participants, please remind them to register their attendance using the attendance link or QR code provided.

For onsite participants, attendance registration is expected to have been completed at the registration area, including the required attendance form accessible through the provided link/Google Form. Session hosts may remind participants to ensure that their attendance has been properly recorded.
Managing Presentations

Each presenter is allocated 12 minutes for their presentation. It is essential to monitor the time closely to ensure that each presenter adheres to this limit. Politely remind presenters of their remaining time at the following intervals:
5 minutes remaining
2 minutes remaining
Time is up
If a presenter appears to be off-track or exceeding their time, intervene tactfully to keep the session on schedule. This may involve providing a discreet reminder or signaling the need to conclude.

Facilitating the Q&A Session After each presentation, initiate the Q&A session (3 minutes) and encourage audience participation by inviting questions. If the audience is hesitant, be prepared to ask insightful questions yourself to stimulate discussion. Ensure that the Q&A is concise and focused, with questions and comments from the audience kept brief to allow for multiple interactions. A Certificate of Presentation will be provided to the presenter after the completion of their presentation and Q&A.

Awarding of Certificates After all paper presentations have been completed, certificates will be awarded to each presenter. Please ensure that a photo opportunity is arranged for each presenter upon receiving their certificate. After all certificates have been awarded, a group photo of all presenters and the awarding committee/organizers should also be taken.

Concluding the Session As the session concludes, thank the presenters and the audience for their contributions. Summarize any key points or themes that emerged during the presentations and discussions. If there are any announcements or logistical details to share, such as upcoming sessions or breaks, provide this information before dismissing the attendees.

Professional Conduct and Courtesy Throughout the session, maintain a professional and courteous demeanor. Your role as a members is not only to manage time but also to create a respectful and engaging environment. Ensure that all interactions are conducted in a manner that reflects the conference's standards of academic excellence and inclusivity.

By following these guidelines, you will play a crucial role in ensuring that the sessions are both informative and well-organized, contributing to the overall success of MIRC 2026. Your leadership and attention to detail are greatly appreciated.

see.name: Ayuntamiento de Manila
see.feeNote: A working government building; interior access is limited
see.where: Andres Soriano Avenue · Plaza de Roma
see.about: The Casas Consistoriales — city hall of Spanish Manila, destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt in 2013 behind its original neoclassical facade. Now the Bureau of the Treasury.

see.name: Bahay Tsinoy
see.where: Anda corner Cabildo Street · Kaisa Heritage Center
see.about: Museum of Chinese life in the Philippines, run by Kaisa Para Sa Kaunlaran. Traces the Tsinoy community from pre-colonial trade through the Parián, the galleon era and the Second World War. Strong on primary material.

see.name: Baluarte de San Andrés
see.where: Muralla Street · South-eastern wall
see.about: A bastion on the south-eastern angle of the walls, one of the quieter points to get up onto the ramparts and see how thick the Spanish defences actually were.

see.name: Baluarte de San Diego
see.where: Muralla Street · Southern wall
see.about: A circular bastion begun in 1586 to a design by the Jesuit Antonio Sedeño — among the oldest stone fortifications in the country. Excavated ruins now sit inside landscaped gardens, and you can walk the rampart.

see.name: Casa Manila
see.where: General Luna Street · Plaza San Luis Complex
see.about: A 1980s reconstruction of an 1850s colonial merchant house, furnished room by room to show how a wealthy Manila family lived — from the caída and sala down to the paired lavatories.

see.name: Fort Santiago
see.where: Santa Clara Street · Northern tip, by the Pasig River
see.about: The Spanish citadel guarding the mouth of the Pasig, begun 1571 on the site of Rajah Sulayman's settlement. José Rizal was held here before his execution in 1896; brass footsteps trace his last walk across the courtyard. The pin marks the main gate, where tickets are sold.

see.name: Manila Cathedral
see.feeNote: Closed to sightseers during Mass and weddings
see.where: Cabildo corner Beaterio Street · Plaza de Roma
see.about: The Minor Basilica of the Immaculate Conception. The present building, finished in 1958, is the eighth on this site — its predecessors were taken in turn by fire, typhoon, earthquake and the 1945 battle. Belgian stained glass and a Dutch pipe organ.

see.name: Memorare — Manila 1945
see.where: Anda Street · Plazuela de Santa Isabel
see.about: Peter de Guzman's 1995 memorial to the roughly 100,000 civilians killed in the month-long Battle of Manila. A huddled group of figures beneath a grieving woman, with an inscription worth reading in full — the most affecting thing in Intramuros.

see.name: Museo de Intramuros
see.where: Arzobispo corner Anda Street · Reconstructed San Ignacio Church
see.about: The Intramuros Administration's ecclesiastical art collection, opened 2019 inside the rebuilt shell of San Ignacio Church. Colonial santos, retablos and ivory carvings, shown in a deliberately modern interior.

see.name: Plaza de Roma
see.where: Cabildo Street · Between the Cathedral and the Ayuntamiento
see.about: The main square of Spanish Manila and the natural place to start. It was a bullring until the 1790s, then Plaza McKinley under the Americans, renamed Plaza de Roma in 1961. The King Charles IV monument stands at its centre.

see.name: Plaza México
see.where: Aduana Street · Northern quarter, near the river
see.about: A square commemorating the Manila–Acapulco galleon trade, which ran between these two ports for 250 years and made Intramuros the hinge of the first genuinely global trade route.

see.name: Plaza Moriones
see.feeNote: Covered by the Fort Santiago ticket
see.where: Inside Fort Santiago · Fort Santiago
see.about: The old parade ground inside Fort Santiago, now lawn and acacia. The open space that makes the fort a pleasant place to sit rather than only to tour.

see.name: Plazuela de Santa Isabel
see.where: Anda corner Real Street · Central Intramuros
see.about: The small square that holds the Memorare monument, on the site of the Colegio de Santa Isabel — one of the oldest schools for girls in Asia.

see.name: Postigo del Palacio
see.where: Muralla Street · Western wall
see.about: The Postern of the Palace — the Governor-General's private gate to the river and the bay, small enough to be missed and carrying a relief of Our Lady of Solitude above the arch.

see.name: Puerta de Isabel II
see.where: Magallanes Drive · Northern wall
see.about: Opened in 1861 and named for Queen Isabella II of Spain, whose statue once stood before it. The newest of the original gates, cut to ease traffic to the river district.

see.name: Puerta de Santa Lucia
see.where: Santa Lucia Street · Western wall, facing Manila Bay
see.about: A western gate opening toward the bay, with one of the better-preserved stretches of curtain wall and a ravelin still in front of it.

see.name: Puerta Real
see.where: Muralla Street · Southern wall
see.about: The Royal Gate, reserved for the Governor-General and opened only on ceremonial occasions. Rebuilt in the 1960s; the sunken gardens beside it are a good quiet stop.

see.name: Rizal Shrine
see.where: Inside Fort Santiago · Fort Santiago
see.about: Museum in the barracks where Rizal spent his final hours, holding his manuscripts, personal effects and the original of "Mi Último Adiós", smuggled out in an oil lamp.

see.name: San Agustin Church
see.feeNote: The adjoining museum is ticketed separately
see.hours: Daily, roughly 8am–6pm (closed to visitors during Mass and weddings)
see.where: General Luna Street · Opposite Plaza San Luis
see.about: Completed in 1607, the oldest stone church in the Philippines and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was the only Intramuros church left standing after the 1945 Battle of Manila. The barrel-vaulted ceiling is a trompe-l'œil painted flat in 1875.

see.name: San Agustin Museum
see.feeNote: ₱160 for students, seniors, PWD and frontliners
see.where: General Luna Street · Augustinian monastery, beside the church
see.about: The monastery beside San Agustin, now a museum of religious art, vestments and colonial-era furniture arranged around two storeys of cloisters. Quiet, and the best single introduction to Spanish-era ecclesiastical Manila.

see.name: Santa Lucia Barracks Ruins
see.where: Santa Lucia Street · Southern quarter
see.about: What is left of the Spanish infantry barracks, flattened in 1945 and deliberately left unreconstructed. The clearest surviving evidence in Intramuros of how total the destruction was.
